p.src: The historical point should be stated accurately. Ernst Ising solved the one-dimensional model assigned by Wilhelm Lenz and correctly found no finite-temperature phase transition. The overreach was the inference that the same conclusion should hold in every dimension. It does not. The two-dimensional model already has an ordered low-temperature phase.

p.src: An exact solution in higher dimension is too ambitious for the present purpose. A physically transparent approximation will be enough to expose the transition when each spin has many neighbors. Before making that approximation, however, it is worth solving the one-dimensional chain exactly. The contrast between the exact one-dimensional answer and the high-dimensional approximation identifies the mechanism that one dimension lacks.

p.src: A phase transition here means more than a gradual strengthening of an existing preference. As temperature crosses a critical value, the equilibrium state acquires a new macroscopic property: a nonzero magnetization can persist even after the external field used to orient the sample has been removed. The calculation must therefore answer two separate questions. Does a distant spin remember the orientation of a chosen spin, and can an infinitesimal field organize an arbitrarily large sample?

p.src:
Take a two-state variable $\sigma=\pm1,$ and choose the energy convention $E(\sigma)=-J\sigma,
\qquad J>0.$ The state $\sigma=+1$ then has lower energy. The parameter $J$ may stand for a magnetic moment multiplied by an applied field, but only the product enters this calculation.

p.src: The One-Dimensional Chain

u.src: The One-Dimensional Chain
en: The One-Dimensional Chain

p.src:
Place $N$ spins on an open chain and let neighboring spins interact: $H=-J\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1},
\qquad \sigma_i=\pm1.$ For $J>0$, a parallel pair contributes $-J$, while an antiparallel pair contributes $+J$. The two ground states are therefore $(+,+,\ldots,+)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
(-,-,\ldots,-).$

p.src: Changing $J$ to $-J$ favors alternating spins. On an open chain, or on an even periodic chain, the redefinition $\widetilde{\sigma}_i=(-1)^i\sigma_i$ maps the antiferromagnetic sign back to the ferromagnetic one. The distinction is physical, but the one-dimensional partition-function algebra is the same. An odd periodic chain is the familiar exception because it cannot alternate without frustration.

p.src: Memory as a correlation function

u.src: Memory as a correlation function
en: Memory as a correlation function

p.src: Suppose $\sigma_i$ is known to be up. Does that information influence a spin $r$ bonds away? The diagnostic is $C(r)=\expect{\sigma_i\sigma_{i+r}}.$ If $C(r)$ approaches a nonzero number as $r\to\infty$, the system retains long-range memory. If it approaches zero, the effect of the first spin eventually disappears.

p.src: The game of telephone gives the right intuition. Each person transmits one binary symbol to the next. If every transmission is perfect, the initial bit survives indefinitely. If each step has any nonzero error probability, repeated transmission eventually loses the original message. Zero temperature is the perfect-transmission limit of the Ising chain. Any positive temperature permits occasional disagreements between neighbors.

p.src: For a numerical picture, suppose a single transmission has fidelity $0.99$. Two perfect transmissions occur with probability $0.99^2=0.9801$, and each additional step supplies another factor of $0.99$. A hundred steps already make errors common; ten thousand steps erase practical memory. The Ising chain uses a signed measure of fidelity rather than this no-error probability, but the multiplicative loss is the same idea.

=p-(1-p)=2p-1.$ Thus the quantity multiplied from link to link is the excess fidelity $2p-1$, not $p$ itself.

p.src: Bond Variables and the Exact Partition Function

u.src: Bond Variables and the Exact Partition Function
en: Bond Variables and the Exact Partition Function

p.src:
The decisive change of variables is to describe relationships rather than individual spins: $\mu_i=\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1},
\qquad i=1,\ldots,N-1.$ Each bond variable is $+1$ for agreement and $-1$ for disagreement. If the first spin is fixed, the bonds determine every later spin: $\begin{aligned}
\sigma_2&=\sigma_1\mu_1,\\
\sigma_3&=\sigma_1\mu_1\mu_2,\\
\sigma_{r+1}&=\sigma_1\prod_{k=1}^{r}\mu_k.\end{aligned}$ There is no redundancy. The data $(\sigma_1,\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_{N-1})$ are equivalent to $(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_N)$.

p.src: The leading factor of two is the global choice of the first spin. It contributes only $\log2$ to $\log Z_N$, while the bonds contribute a term proportional to $N-1$. The factor matters for exact finite-size counting but disappears from the free-energy density as $N\to\infty$. This is why the board could call it "no big deal" without actually discarding it.

This site-bond exchange is a modest example of a pattern that becomes much more powerful in higher-dimensional statistical mechanics.

p.src: At every finite temperature, $0<\tanh(\beta J)<1,$ so memory decays exponentially. Writing $C(r)=e^{-r/\xi}$ defines the exact correlation length $\xi^{-1}=-\log\!\left[\tanh(\beta J)\right].$ Only at $T=0$ does $\xi$ diverge. At low but nonzero temperature, $\xi\simeq \frac{1}{2}e^{2\beta J},$ so the chain can contain very long aligned stretches without possessing true infinite-range order.

p.src: One dimension provides no error correction. Once a bond disagrees with its predecessor, the next spin has no independent source telling it which orientation was intended. The chain therefore consists of long aligned domains separated by occasional switches.

p.src: In a square lattice each site has four nearest neighbors. In a cubic lattice it has six. On a $d$-dimensional hypercubic lattice it has $z=2d$ nearest neighbors. A site receiving three agreeing messages and one disagreeing message can follow the majority. The many-neighbor environment suppresses isolated errors in much the same way that redundant messages enable error correction.

p.src:
If the neighbors have mean spin $m$, their sum has mean $zm$. Its ordinary fluctuation is of order $\sqrt{z}$, so away from $m=0$ the relative fluctuation scales approximately as $\frac{\sqrt{z}}{z|m|}
=\frac{1}{\sqrt{z}\,|m|}.$ This is why an average field becomes plausible at large coordination number. It also warns us that the approximation becomes least reliable near a critical point, where $m$ is small.

p.src: A remembered saying captures the large-number intuition: a hundred independent votes are unlikely to be wrong in the same direction. The quantitative version is the square-root law. A coherent bias in $z$ variables is proportional to $z$, while random disagreement is typically proportional only to $\sqrt{z}$. Increasing dimension therefore changes not only the number of neighbors but the reliability of their collective message.

p.src: Mean Field as a Self-Consistency Problem

u.src: Mean Field as a Self-Consistency Problem
en: Mean Field as a Self-Consistency Problem

p.src:
Focus on one spin $\sigma_i$. Its interaction with its $z=2d$ neighbors is $E_i=-J\sigma_i\sum_{j\in{\rm nn}(i)}\sigma_j.$ Let $m=\expect{\sigma}$ denote the uniform magnetization per spin. Mean field replaces the fluctuating neighbor sum by its average: $\sum_{j\in{\rm nn}(i)}\sigma_j
\longrightarrow zm=2dm.$ The distinguished spin then has the effective one-spin energy $E_i^{\rm MF}=-2dJm\,\sigma_i.$

p.src:
The one-spin result can now be reused with the effective field $2dJm$: $\expect{\sigma_i}_{\rm effective}
=\tanh(2\beta dJm).$ But the selected site is not special. Translation invariance requires its average to equal the assumed average $m$. Hence $\boxed{m=\tanh(2\beta dJm)}.$ This is why mean field is also called the self-consistent-field approximation: the magnetization that creates the effective field must equal the magnetization produced by that field.

p.src:
Define $K=2\beta dJ,
\qquad
y=Km.$ Then Equation  becomes $\frac{y}{K}=\tanh y.$ The right side is a fixed sigmoid. The left side is a line through the origin with slope $\frac{1}{K}=\frac{T}{2dJ},$ where $k_{\rm B}=1$.

Define $K=2\beta dJ,
\qquad
y=Km.$ Then Equation  becomes $\frac{y}{K}=\tanh y.$ The right side is a fixed sigmoid. The left side is a line through the origin with slope $\frac{1}{K}=\frac{T}{2dJ},$ where $k_{\rm B}=1$.

p.src:
At high temperature the line is steep and intersects $\tanh y$ only at $y=0$. At low temperature the line is shallow and there are three intersections: $y=0$ and a symmetric pair $y=\pm y_0$. The threshold occurs when the line and $\tanh y$ have the same slope at the origin. Since $\tanh'(0)=1$, $K_c=1,
\qquad
T_c^{\rm MF}=2dJ.$ This is the mean-field critical temperature, not the exact answer in low dimension.

\qquad
T_c^{\rm MF}=2dJ.$ This is the mean-field critical temperature, not the exact answer in low dimension.

p.src: The assumption $J>0$ says that neighboring spins prefer to agree; it does not select $+m$ over $-m$. At zero external field the Hamiltonian is unchanged by the global flip $\sigma_i\mapsto-\sigma_i$, so the two nonzero intersections are physically equivalent. Choosing only the positive half of the graph is a convenient drawing convention, not a loss of the negative phase.

p.src: Start from the all-up state. A broken bond changes its energy from $-J$ to $+J$, so each broken bond costs $\Delta E_{\rm bond}=2J.$ On a square lattice, one flipped spin breaks four bonds and costs $8J$. Two adjacent flipped spins have a perimeter of six broken bonds and cost $12J$, whereas two far-separated flips break eight bonds and cost $16J$.

p.src: There are of order $N^2$ ways to choose the two walls of such a block in a chain of $N$ sites. Their energy does not grow with the separation between the walls. At any positive temperature, entropy therefore supplies arbitrarily large reversed domains. In two dimensions the boundary energy can defeat the contour entropy at sufficiently low temperature. This energy-entropy competition is the geometric fact that mean field cannot see when it treats $d=1$ and $d=2$ merely as different numerical values of the same coefficient.

p.src: An External Field Selects the Phase

u.src: An External Field Selects the Phase
en: An External Field Selects the Phase

p.src:
Add a uniform field $h$ with the convention that $h>0$ favors $\sigma=+1$: $H=-J\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}\sigma_i\sigma_j
-h\sum_i\sigma_i.$ The mean-field energy of one selected spin is $E_i^{\rm MF}=-(2dJm+h)\sigma_i,$ and the self-consistency equation becomes $\boxed{m=\tanh\!\left[\beta(2dJm+h)\right]}.$ With $K=2\beta dJ$ and $y=Km$, $\frac{y}{K}=\tanh(y+\beta h).$

p.src:
The proper statement requires an order of limits. A finite system at exactly $h=0$ has spin-flip symmetry and therefore $\expect{m}=0$ in the full equilibrium ensemble. Spontaneous magnetization is $m_{\rm sp}
=\lim_{h\to0^+}\lim_{N\to\infty}\expect{m}_{N,h},$ with the thermodynamic limit taken first. Reversing the sign of the infinitesimal field gives $-m_{\rm sp}$. The total field-energy difference is proportional to $Nh$, so even a tiny field becomes decisive for a macroscopic sample.

p.src: A Magnetic Reversal Is a Different Problem

u.src: A Magnetic Reversal Is a Different Problem
en: A Magnetic Reversal Is a Different Problem

p.src:
The exact chain and the mean-field lattice now give two sharply different answers. In one dimension, $\expect{\sigma_i\sigma_{i+r}}
=\left[\tanh(\beta J)\right]^r
\longrightarrow0
\qquad (T>0),$ because finite-energy domain walls can separate arbitrarily long reversed intervals. With many neighbors, the self-consistent field instead admits stable nonzero solutions below $T_c^{\rm MF}=2dJ.$ The contrast is not merely algebraic. It is the competition among geometry, energy, entropy, and redundancy: whether an error can spread freely or whether the surrounding lattice can correct it.
